name: Execute a planned thermal unit outage
summary: During a planned outage a converted gas unit or cogeneration plant is shut down, isolated and opened; company specialist crews and contractor crews inspect, repair and reassemble the turbine, boiler and auxiliaries on two shifts, and the unit is tested and returned to the market. Outage managers and planners run the schedule, plant engineers and inspectors decide on repairs, operators isolate and restart the unit and safety advisors run orientation and incident response. Discovered work, late parts, failed pressure tests and start-up problems extend outages, and every extra day is lost market revenue.

baseline.org_archetype: An Alberta merchant generator with about 1,300 staff, three gas steam units converted from coal at the Wabamun-area sites, two cogeneration plants, 17 hydro plants and 12 wind farms, with a central engineering and asset management division of about 130 people.
baseline.notes: Reference period 2019 to 2022. Minor outages last one to three weeks; majors with turbine opening last six to nine weeks.

unit_of_work: one planned thermal or cogeneration unit outage (major or minor)
trigger: The outage plan is issued and contractors begin to mobilise for the scheduled shutdown.
end_state: The unit is back in the market, the condition report is written and the outage is closed out.

volume.seasonality: Outages are concentrated in April to June and September to November.

evidence.note: TransAlta reported two planned major outages on Alberta coal units in 2019, one in 2018 and four in 2017 (tac2019mda); adding annual minors on three converted units and two cogeneration plants gives about 8 to 12 thermal outages a year. The organisation file's 1/3/8 per month is too high for outages of this kind.

surge.cause: spring and fall planned outage seasons

evidence.note: Kept from the organisation file: outages are placed in shoulder seasons when Alberta demand and prices are lower.
Four outage managers share execution, planning and AESO reporting.
Planners on shift during outages for schedule updates and timesheets.
Specialist crew leads on outages.

26 technicians; about a quarter of their time on thermal outages, the rest on routine crew dispatch and hydro work. A crew of six works in parallel, so person-hours are about six times the elapsed hours in s05 and s11.
Mobile and turbine hall crane lifts during outages.
Orientation and incident response during outages.
Shutdown, isolation and return to service; not listed in the organisation file's roles for this process.
Start-up tests; not listed in the organisation file's roles for this process.
Repair decisions and inspection sign-off; not listed in the organisation file's roles for this process.
Condition reports; not listed in the organisation file's roles for this process.

systems.name: ERP (finance, purchasing and plant maintenance modules)
Outage and project scheduling software (critical path)
AESO Energy Trading System (offers, declarations and dispatch)
Document management and engineering drawings repository

resources.name: Gas-fired steam unit converted from coal (about 400 to 460 MW)

steps.name: Mobilise contractors and run site orientation
steps.description: In the week before shutdown the safety advisor runs site orientations for arriving contractor crews (often several hundred workers for a major), checks training records and tickets, issues site access and explains the outage safety plan, muster points and confined-space rescue arrangements.

control.basis: Alberta OHS Act and Code worker orientation and training duties; company contractor safety standard

evidence.note: Contractor orientation before outage start is common practice; several hundred workers on a major is the organisation file's description.

steps.name: Shut down unit and hand over to the outage
steps.description: At the scheduled hour the shift supervisor ramps the unit down under AESO dispatch, trips the turbine, puts it on turning gear and records the hand-over of the unit from operations to the outage team. The unit stays out of the market until return to service.

evidence.note: Standard shutdown practice; the unit is held for the whole outage (resource occupancy: 8 to 60 days, see s09 for the major-outage path).

steps.name: Request isolations and permits
steps.description: The crew lead submits permit requests in the permit-to-work system for each work package against the prepared isolation lists, starting with the systems on the critical path, and confirms the order of isolation with the shift supervisor.

control.basis: Alberta OHS Code Part 15 ss. 212-214 control of hazardous energy; company permit-to-work standard

evidence.note: Isolation before work is required (ohs15); the permits themselves are issued in gas-issue-work-permits.

steps.name: Open up boiler and equipment
steps.description: Contractor crews erect scaffolding inside the furnace and around the turbine, remove insulation and lagging, open manways and drain systems once the permits are live and the boiler and turbine have cooled enough to enter.

next.condition: major outage: turbine to be opened

evidence.note: Cool-down and isolation before entry take one to several days; elapsed working hours estimated.

steps.name: Open turbine and repair rotors at laydown
steps.description: On a major outage the specialist crew unbolts the turbine casings and, with the turbine hall crane, lifts the upper casings and removes the high, intermediate and low pressure rotors to laydown, then cleans them and repairs blades and seals at laydown, working two 10- to 12-hour shifts. This step carries the extra turbine time of a major.

evidence.note: Turbine work on a major runs 25 to 38 days for full replacements (pe2009); disassembly hours estimated.

steps.name: Inspect components and run NDE
steps.description: OEM field engineers and NDE contractors inspect blades, seals, valves and boiler tubes with visual, ultrasonic, magnetic particle and thickness testing and record findings with photos against the inspection plan.

evidence.note: OEM and NDE inspection during outages is common practice; elapsed hours estimated.

steps.name: Assess findings and decide repairs
steps.description: The plant engineer, with the reliability engineer and OEM representative, compares findings with acceptance criteria and OEM guidance and decides for each item whether to repair, replace, run as is or defer, which often adds discovered work to the schedule.

error.defect_description: A defect accepted as run-as-is that later causes a forced outage.

evidence.note: Emergent work is a known outage risk (powermag2014); the 45 percent share is the author's estimate.

steps.name: Approve discovered work
steps.description: The outage manager reviews each discovered work item for cost, schedule impact and risk of leaving it, approves it within the outage contingency or escalates it, and issues change orders to contractors.

control.basis: Outage scope change control and delegation of financial authority

next.condition: can be done with parts on hand

evidence.note: Outage change control is common practice.

steps.name: Wait for expedited parts or shop repair
steps.description: Supply chain and the OEM expedite replacement parts or ship components to a repair shop; the outage team waits while work continues elsewhere, and the return date often sets the new critical path.

evidence.note: Long-lead parts named as typical delay (powermag2014); durations estimated.

steps.name: Update the critical-path schedule
steps.description: The outage planner collects progress from each crew every shift, enters percent complete and new work into the scheduling tool, recalculates the critical path and the forecast return-to-service date, and issues the updated schedule for the next shift meeting.

evidence.note: Shift-by-shift schedule updates are common practice in outages.

steps.name: Repair and reassemble turbine and valves
steps.description: The specialist crew repairs or replaces blades, seals and valve internals, sets clearances, reinstalls rotors and casings with the turbine hall crane, aligns the shaft train and torques the bolting, recording as-left readings at each hold point.

error.defect_description: Clearance, alignment or bolting error found at start-up testing.

evidence.note: Turbine replacements of 25 to 38 days on majors (pe2009); minor outages need only valve and auxiliary work. Elapsed shift hours estimated.

steps.name: Repair boiler and auxiliaries
steps.description: Contractor crews replace or pad-weld boiler tubes, repair burners, fans, air heaters and pumps, and close up the boiler, working in parallel with the turbine work under their own permits.

error.defect_description: Weld or tube repair that fails the pressure test.

evidence.note: Boiler majors of 45 days or more (pe2009) and a 42-day outage with boiler inspection and repair (iir2003); elapsed hours here exclude time already counted in the parallel turbine work.

steps.name: Make outdoor lifts with the mobile crane
steps.description: The crane operator sets up the hydraulic mobile crane for lifts outside the turbine hall (fan motors, transformer parts, valves to the boiler roof), following the lift plan, and stops when wind speed exceeds the crane's limit.

control.basis: Alberta OHS Code Part 6 cranes, hoists and lifting devices; company critical lift procedure

evidence.note: Outdoor crane lifts are limited by wind; hours estimated.

steps.name: Run shift coordination and safety meetings
steps.description: The outage manager chairs the start-of-shift meeting with crew leads, contractors and operations: safety topics, permits for the shift, critical-path progress and blockers. The time here is the total over the outage.

next.condition: safety incident or near miss reported

evidence.note: Daily outage meetings are common practice; incident share estimated.

steps.name: Report and investigate an incident
steps.description: The safety advisor records the incident or near miss in the incident system, secures the scene, interviews the workers and contractor supervisor, notifies Alberta OHS if the incident is serious and passes the report to the incident investigation process.

control.basis: Alberta OHS Act serious incident reporting

evidence.note: Incident reporting duties under the Alberta OHS Act; hours estimated.

steps.name: Get pressure equipment inspection sign-off
steps.description: The plant engineer walks the boiler and pressure piping repairs with the inspector, reviews weld records and NDE reports, witnesses the hydrostatic test and gets the inspection signed before the boiler can be closed and fired.

control.basis: Alberta Pressure Equipment Safety Regulation; ABSA inspection of repairs and alterations

evidence.note: Boiler repairs are inspected under ABSA rules before return to service; rejection share estimated.

steps.name: Close work orders and surrender permits
steps.description: The crew lead confirms each job is complete and the area clean, records hours and as-left notes on the work orders in the ERP and signs off the permits so the systems can be returned to operations.

control.basis: Alberta OHS Code Part 15 ss. 212-214 control of hazardous energy; company permit-to-work standard

evidence.note: Permits are surrendered before isolation is removed (ohs15); hours estimated.

steps.name: Remove locks and return systems to operations
steps.description: The shift supervisor checks that all personal locks are removed and permits surrendered, removes the isolations in sequence, refills and vents systems and returns each system to operations.

control.basis: Alberta OHS Code Part 15 ss. 212-214 control of hazardous energy; company permit-to-work standard

evidence.note: Personal locks and verification of isolation (ohs15).

steps.name: Start up and run hold-point tests
steps.description: Control room operators fire the boiler, roll the turbine and run the post-outage tests: valve stroking, overspeed trip, vibration checks and protection checks, stopping to fix anything that fails.

evidence.note: Start-up test sequence is common practice; failure share estimated.

steps.name: Synchronise and declare the unit available
steps.description: The shift supervisor synchronises the unit to the grid, tells the real-time desk the unit is back and the available MW so offers and availability can be restated, and logs the end of the outage.

control.basis: AESO ISO rules on available capability and outage completion

evidence.note: Return-to-service notification to the trading desk and the AESO.

steps.name: Request capability and heat-rate test
steps.description: The plant engineer sends a test request to the performance testing process so the unit's capability and heat rate after the outage can be measured and declared.

evidence.note: The organisation file links outage execution to performance testing.

steps.name: Demobilise contractors and release cranes
steps.description: The crew lead releases contractor crews in stages, returns rental equipment, releases the cranes and specialist crews for other sites and checks that laydown areas are cleared.

evidence.note: Common practice.

steps.name: Reconcile timesheets and change orders
steps.description: The outage planner checks contractor timesheets and change order claims against daily logs and approved changes, queries differences and approves the totals; company overtime timesheets go to payroll.

control.basis: Internal control over contractor invoices: approval against field records

evidence.note: Timesheet reconciliation after outages is common practice.

steps.name: Write as-found and as-left condition report
steps.description: The reliability engineer compiles inspection findings, repairs, measurements and deferred items into the outage condition report and recommends follow-up inspections and maintenance strategy changes.

evidence.note: The organisation file links execution to reliability analysis through the condition report.

steps.name: Hold lessons-learned review and close the outage
steps.description: The outage manager holds the lessons-learned meeting, compares actual duration and cost with plan, records lessons for the next outage on this unit and closes the outage cost collector.

evidence.note: Common practice.

exceptions.name: Discovered work needing parts
exceptions.description: Inspection finds damage beyond the planned scope and the replacement part or shop repair sets a new critical path.

exceptions.name: Failed start-up test
exceptions.description: Vibration, a leaking valve or a protection fault at start-up sends crews back into the turbine or valves.

exceptions.name: Rejected pressure part repair
exceptions.description: A boiler tube or piping repair fails inspection or the hydrostatic test and is redone.

exceptions.name: Safety incident
exceptions.description: An injury or significant near miss is reported and investigated during the outage.

benchmarks.unit: calendar days from contractor mobilisation to outage closeout
benchmarks.population: Planned thermal unit outages, mix of about three minors to one major

evidence.note: Author's estimate built from outage durations (minor 8 to 21 days, major 42 to 60 days, pe2009 and iir2003) plus about a week of mobilisation and three to six weeks of closeout (timesheets, condition report, lessons learned). With about three minors to each major the median is near 60 days.

benchmarks.unit: days from shutdown to return to service
benchmarks.population: Coal-fired steam units with boiler and turbine work

evidence.note: Boiler major 45 days or more (pe2009); 42-day outage on a 323 MW unit (iir2003).

benchmarks.population: TransAlta Keephills 2, Keephills 3 and Sundance 6 conversions, 2021

evidence.note: Conversions were done during planned outages.

pain_points.description: Discovered work found after opening, and the parts it needs, sets a new critical path and delays return to market.

evidence.note: Emergent work and long-lead parts named as main outage risks.

pain_points.description: Shared specialist crews and cranes move between sites, so a slip on one outage delays turbine work on another.

evidence.note: Four crews and two owned cranes in the organisation file serve all sites.

pain_points.description: Start-up test failures send crews back after systems have been returned, repeating permits and isolations.

evidence.note: Author's estimate.

pain_points.description: Contractor timesheets and change orders are reconciled by hand against paper daily logs weeks after the outage.

evidence.note: Author's estimate of 2019-2022 practice.

assumptions: Touch time on crew steps (s04, s05, s06, s11, s12) is elapsed working time of the crew on two shifts, not summed person-hours, so that the simulated cycle reflects the outage duration. Person-hours are several times higher, which is why stated FTE exceed the FTE implied by touch time.

Parallel work (boiler, turbine, crane lifts, daily meetings) is listed in sequence with near-zero waits and named in concurrent_with; the parallel steps carry only the time not already covered by the critical path.
The converted unit is held for the outage duration; it is listed without a running cost because it burns no fuel while offline. Lost market margin is not modelled.
Hydro and wind unit outages are executed by their divisions and are not part of this file's volume.
Loaded costs are taken from the organisation file (wage x 1.40). Contractor labour is not costed because contractor steps use the role external.

The simulated median (about 76 days) sits above the 60-day benchmark and the p90 (about 93 days) below the 105-day benchmark. The simulator draws each step's time independently, so major-outage cases do not also get long repair, test and closeout times, and office touch time (timesheets, reports) is counted as continuous elapsed time. The spread between minor and major outages is therefore narrower than in practice.
The roles state about 13 FTE against about 4 FTE implied by touch time because crew steps record elapsed crew time, not the person-hours of six-person crews (see the first assumption).

sources.title: Critical Path: Getting Your Outage Ducks in a Row (A. Larson)
sources.supports: Outage preparation is continuous and can be a full-time department; major projects are planned years ahead; scope is frozen early and contractors estimate and schedule only after the freeze; readiness meetings 90, 60 and 30 days before shutdown with tasks coded green, yellow or red; long-lead parts are a typical red item; unready tasks go on a risk register; scope creep and emergent work are the main threat.

sources.title: TransAlta Corporation Management's Discussion and Analysis for 2019 (Exhibit 13.2 to Form 40-F)
sources.publisher: TransAlta Corporation via U.S. SEC EDGAR
sources.supports: Canadian Coal planned major maintenance 34 million CAD in 2019, 15 million in 2018, 54 million in 2017; two planned major outages (Keephills 1 and Sundance 4) in 2019, one planned major outage at a non-operated unit in 2018 and four planned outages in 2017; Canadian Gas planned major maintenance 8, 16 and 22 million; consolidated sustaining capital 141 million CAD (2019), 150 million (2018), 218 million (2017) and 170 to 200 million forecast for 2020.

sources.title: TransAlta Corporation 2021 Integrated Report (Form 6-K)
sources.publisher: TransAlta Corporation via U.S. SEC EDGAR
sources.supports: Coal-to-gas conversions completed 2020-2021 at 7 to 39 million CAD per unit (Keephills 3 31 million, Keephills 2 34 million, Sundance 6 39 million); planned outages for the Keephills 2 and 3 boiler conversions reduced 2021 adjusted availability to 86.6 percent; planned major maintenance is part of sustaining capital; 2022 sustaining capital assumption 150 to 170 million CAD; significant planned major outages expected in 2022.

sources.title: Short-term Fixes Often Trump Major Component Replacements (S. Blankinship)
sources.supports: Major work at coal plants is done as a capital outage scheduled with a major boiler inspection and repair every three years or so; a typical boiler major lasts 45 days or longer; a high-pressure turbine can be replaced in about 25 days and a low-pressure turbine in 35 to 38 days; modern designs allow about 100,000 hours between low-pressure turbine inspections.

sources.title: April Outage Scheduled for Warrick Generating Station
sources.supports: A 42-day planned outage on a 323 MW coal unit covering boiler inspection and repair, steam turbine-generator, feedwater heating, cooling tower, fuel and ash handling and SCR tie-ins.

sources.title: Occupational Health and Safety Code, Part 15 Managing the Control of Hazardous Energy (Alberta Regulation 191/2021)
sources.supports: Part 15 requires isolation of machinery and equipment before work (s. 212), verification of isolation (s. 213), personal locks (s. 214) and rules for securing by individual workers and groups. The same Part existed in the earlier Code (AR 87/2009) in force in 2019 to 2021.
